item.title: Big O Calculator for JavaScript: Time and Space Complexity
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Mustafa
item.description: Use a Big O calculator for JavaScript the right way: read time and space complexity from loops, array and string methods, with real code examples.
item.content:encoded:
A Big O calculator for JavaScript is only useful if it shows its work. I built Complexity Coach, a free tool that reads your code and estimates its time and space complexity, because most answers I found online were either a bare "O(n)" with no reason or a confident guess.

In this guide I explain how Big O notation maps to real JavaScript, which built-in methods hide extra cost, how time and space complexity differ, and where a static calculator, including mine, should refuse to guess.

Big O notation in plain words

Big O describes how the work grows when the input grows. It ignores the exact number of milliseconds, because that depends on the machine. It only asks: if the input doubles, what happens to the work?

  • O(1): the work stays the same, like reading arr[5].
  • O(log n): the work grows very slowly, like binary search, which halves the range each step.
  • O(n): the work grows with the input, like one loop over an array.
  • O(n log n): typical for good sorting.
  • O(n²): every item compared with every other item, usually two nested loops.

Two rules do most of the work. Drop constants, so O(2n) is just O(n). Keep the biggest term, so O(n² + n) becomes O(n²). The second rule has a catch I will come back to, because it only applies when the terms use the same input.

How to read Big O from JavaScript code

You do not need maths to estimate Big O for most interview or product code. You need to count how many times each line can run.

Loops multiply, separate blocks add

One loop over n items is O(n). A loop inside another loop multiplies: O(n × n), or O(n²). Two loops one after the other add: O(n + n), which is still O(n).

function hasDuplicate(nums) {
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {        // n times
    for (let j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) {  // up to n times each
      if (nums[i] === nums[j]) return true;
    }
  }
  return false;
}
// Time: O(n²)  Extra space: O(1)

Different inputs get different letters

This is the most common mistake I see. If the outer loop runs over comments and the inner loop runs over bannedWords, the answer is O(m × n), not O(n²). Writing n² hides the fact that a long banned-word list hurts just as much as a long comment list.

The same applies to adding terms. O(m × L + n) cannot be simplified to O(m × L), because n is a different input. "Keep the biggest term" only works when the bigger term contains all the same sizes.

Halving means logarithmic

When each step cuts the remaining range in half, like binary search with a mid index, the loop runs about log₂ n times. For a million items, that is around 20 steps.

Recursion needs a recurrence, not a glance

Recursive code is where quick estimates go wrong. Count how many calls each call makes and how deep the calls go. The naive Fibonacci function below calls itself twice per step, so the number of calls roughly doubles at each level:

function fib(n) {
  if (n < 2) return n;
  return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); // two calls per call: about O(2^n)
}

function fibMemo(n, memo = new Map()) {
  if (n < 2) return n;
  if (memo.has(n)) return memo.get(n);
  const value = fibMemo(n - 1, memo) + fibMemo(n - 2, memo);
  memo.set(n, value); // each n is computed once: O(n) time, O(n) space
  return value;
}

The memoised version does the same maths but stores each answer, so every value of n is computed once. The call stack still grows to depth n, which is why its space is O(n), not O(1).

Hidden costs in JavaScript array and string methods

Many JavaScript methods look like one cheap line but contain a loop. A single includes inside a loop is often what turns O(n) code into O(n²).

OperationTimeExtra spaceNote
arr[i], push, popO(1)O(1)push is O(1) on average
includes, indexOf, find, someO(n)O(1)Linear scan of the array
map, filterO(n)O(n)Build a new array
slice, concat, [...arr]O(k)O(k)Copy k items
shift, unshift, spliceUsually O(n)O(1)Other items move position
sortO(n log n)Up to O(n)V8 uses TimSort
Map / Set get, has, setO(1) on averageOne entry eachHash tables in practice
split, trim, toLowerCase, replaceO(L)O(L)L is the string length

Two of these deserve a source. V8, the engine in Chrome and Node.js, has used TimSort for Array.prototype.sort since version 7.0, which gives O(n log n) in the worst case. For Map and Set, the ECMAScript specification only requires access times that are sublinear on average. Engines use hash tables, so O(1) on average is the honest way to say it.

The fix for a hidden scan is usually a Set:

// Slow: includes scans bannedWords for every word, O(w × b)
const isClean = words.every((word) => !bannedWords.includes(word));

// Fast: build the Set once in O(b), then each lookup is O(1) on average
const banned = new Set(bannedWords);
const isCleanFast = words.every((word) => !banned.has(word));

Two more patterns catch people in code reviews. The first is a queue built on shift(). In a breadth-first search, calling queue.shift() on every step usually moves all remaining items forward, so a loop that looks linear can become O(n²) on large inputs. Keeping a head index and reading queue[head++] avoids the move.

The second is copying inside a loop. Writing acc = [...acc, item] inside reduce copies the whole array on every step, which is also O(n²) time and creates a lot of short-lived garbage. Pushing into one array keeps it at O(n). Neither pattern is wrong for small lists, but both are worth a comment when the list comes from users.

Strings need their own letter. comment.split(" ") reads the whole comment, so its cost depends on the comment's length, not on how many comments there are. I use L for that.

Time and space complexity, including the output

Time complexity counts steps. Space complexity counts extra memory. Interview answers usually separate two kinds of space:

  • Auxiliary space: memory your algorithm needs while working, such as a Set of seen values or a temporary copy.
  • Space including output: auxiliary space plus the array you return.

A function that fills and returns a result array of n items has O(n) total space, but its auxiliary space can still be O(1):

function doubled(nums) {
  const result = new Array(nums.length); // the output: counts only in total space
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    result[i] = nums[i] * 2;             // one index variable: O(1) extra
  }
  return result;
}
// Time: O(n)  Auxiliary space: O(1)  Space including output: O(n)

Mixing these two up is why two people can look at the same code and give different answers that are both partly right. Complexity Coach shows both values side by side for this reason.

How I built Complexity Coach, and where it refuses to guess

Complexity Coach runs in your browser. It parses the code into an abstract syntax tree (AST) with the Acorn parser, so nothing is sent to a server. It then walks the tree, tracks how loops nest, recognises known array, Map, Set and string operations, highlights the lines that drive the result, and gives a confidence level: High, Medium or Manual review needed.

The rule I care about most is that it does not invent answers. Recursion, calls to helper functions it cannot see, loops without a clear bound and dynamic property access all return "Manual review needed" with the reason and the exact line. A wrong O(1) is worse than no answer, because people trust it.

That rule also showed me a gap. When I tested a comment filter that split each comment into words and checked them against a Set of banned words, the tool answered "Manual review needed", because it did not know split(). Honest, but not useful for very common code. I added the common string methods with L as the string length, and the same code now returns O(m × L + n) time, O(n + L) auxiliary space and O(m + n + L) including the output.

The same test exposed a second problem: an earlier version dropped the n term and answered O(m × L). Building a Set of n banned words is real work that the bigger term does not cover, so smaller terms are now kept whenever they use a different input.

Static analysis or a runtime benchmark?

There are two kinds of Big O calculator. Runtime tools, such as the big-o-calculator package on npm, run your function with growing input sizes and fit the timings to a curve. Static tools, like Complexity Coach, read the code without running it.

Runtime measurement sees real data, but timings are noisy because of JIT warm-up and garbage collection, and the result depends on the test inputs you chose. Static analysis explains why the code grows the way it does, but it cannot know the shape of your production data. I use the static estimate while writing and reviewing code, and a benchmark when a specific function is actually slow.

Practical takeaway

Before you trust any Big O calculator, check five things yourself:

  1. Give each input its own letter, so m × n never hides as n².
  2. Multiply nested loops and add separate blocks.
  3. Look inside one-line methods such as includes, slice, sort and split.
  4. Report auxiliary space and space including the output separately.
  5. Treat recursion as a manual task: write the recurrence instead of guessing.

If you want a second opinion with the evidence on each line, paste your function into Complexity Coach; it is one of my free developer tools. If you need help with performance in a real Node.js or SaaS codebase, get in touch.

item.title: OpenAI vs Claude vs Gemini API Pricing: Cost Calculator Guide
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Mustafa
item.description: Compare OpenAI vs Claude vs Gemini API pricing, then turn token rates into monthly cost per user and margin with a worked example and free calculator.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI, Claude and Gemini all publish their API pricing per million tokens, but that number alone does not tell you what an AI feature will cost each month, or whether your subscription price still leaves a profit. I built a free AI API Cost Calculator to turn token prices into a monthly number before choosing a model.

In this guide I compare current OpenAI vs Claude vs Gemini API pricing, show how to turn those rates into cost per user with a worked example, explain what changes the bill more than the model, and how to check your margin before you launch.

OpenAI vs Claude vs Gemini API pricing at a glance

A token is a small piece of text, roughly three quarters of an English word. Providers charge separately for input tokens (what you send), cached input (repeated text the provider has already processed) and output tokens (what the model writes back). The table shows standard-tier rates in US dollars per 1 million tokens, taken from each provider's official pricing page on 11 November 2026.

ModelInputCached inputOutput
OpenAI GPT-6 Luna$0.10$0.01$0.50
OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol$2.00$0.10$10.00
OpenAI GPT-6 Astra$10.00$1.00$50.00
Claude Haiku 5.5 (prompts up to 100K tokens)$0.10$0.01$0.50
Claude Sonnet 5.5$2.00$0.10$10.00
Claude Opus 5.5$4.00$0.20$20.00
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite$0.30$0.03$2.50
Gemini 3.8 Flash (promo until 31 Dec 2026)$0.75$0.075$3.75
Gemini 4 Carbon (promo until 30 Nov 2026)$2.00$0.10$10.00

Check the OpenAI pricing, Claude pricing and Gemini pricing pages before you commit, because rates move. Four details matter more than the headline numbers:

  • Promotions end. Gemini 3.8 Flash doubles to $1.50 input and $7.50 output on 1 January 2027. Gemini 4 Carbon goes to $4.00 and $20.00 on 1 December 2026.
  • "Cached" works differently. On Claude, writing a prompt to the 5-minute cache costs 1.25 times the base input price, and later reads are cheap. Gemini context caching adds an hourly storage fee. Compare the mechanics, not just the column.
  • Long prompts can cost more. OpenAI charges higher rates above 272K input tokens, Claude Haiku 5.5 above 100K and Gemini 3.1 Pro above 200K. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 keep the same rate across their full 1M context.
  • Batch is half price. All three offer roughly 50% off for jobs that can wait, such as nightly summaries.

How to turn API pricing into cost per user

Price per token is the wrong unit for a product decision. What you need is cost per user per month, because that is what your subscription price has to cover. Five numbers get you there:

  1. Input tokens per request. Count everything you send: the system prompt, previous messages, any retrieved documents and the user's message. The system prompt and history are often bigger than the question.
  2. Output tokens per request. Include reasoning or "thinking" tokens. Gemini lists output prices including thinking, and Claude bills thinking as output too.
  3. Requests per user per month. Count API calls, not clicks. An agent that plans, searches and writes can make four or five calls for one user action.
  4. Cached share. The part of the input that repeats exactly, usually the system prompt and fixed instructions.
  5. Rates for the model, from the table above.

The maths is small enough to keep in your codebase next to the feature:

function monthlyApiCost({ users, requestsPerUser, inputTokens, outputTokens, cachedShare, rates }) {
  const requests = users * requestsPerUser;
  const input = requests * inputTokens;
  const cached = input * cachedShare;      // billed at the cached rate
  const uncached = input - cached;         // billed at the full input rate
  const output = requests * outputTokens;  // usually the biggest line
  return (uncached * rates.input + cached * rates.cached + output * rates.output) / 1_000_000;
}

// 1,000 users, 80 requests each, 2,500 tokens in, 500 out, 40% cached
monthlyApiCost({ users: 1000, requestsPerUser: 80, inputTokens: 2500, outputTokens: 500,
  cachedShare: 0.4, rates: { input: 2, cached: 0.1, output: 10 } }); // 648

A worked example: a support assistant

These are the numbers from the calculator's "Support" preset: 1,000 users, 80 requests each per month, 2,500 input tokens and 500 output tokens per request, with 40% of input cached. That is 80,000 requests, 200 million input tokens and 40 million output tokens a month.

ModelMonthly API costPer user
GPT-6 Luna or Claude Haiku 5.5$32.80$0.03
Gemini 3.8 Flash (promo price)$246$0.25
Gemini 3.8 Flash (from January 2027)$492$0.49
GPT-6.1 Sol or Claude Sonnet 5.5$648$0.65
Claude Opus 5.5$1,296$1.30
GPT-6 Astra$3,280$3.28

Three things stand out. Output is only one sixth of the tokens but about 62% of the bill, because output costs five times the input rate. The cheapest tier is about 20 times cheaper than the mid tier, so the first question is whether a small model is good enough for the task. And GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 cost exactly the same here, so between those two the decision is about answer quality, speed and tooling, not price.

What changes the bill more than the model

Switching models is the obvious lever, but in my experience the shape of each request matters as much. These are the levers I check before blaming the price list.

Output length

Since output dominates the bill, asking for shorter answers and setting a sensible maximum output length is often the cheapest saving. A support reply rarely needs 800 tokens.

Conversation history

Chat APIs are stateless, so each turn usually resends the earlier messages. Input grows with every turn, which means the tenth message in a conversation can cost several times the first. Trimming or summarising older turns keeps that growth in check.

Prompt caching

Put stable content first: the system prompt, tool definitions and fixed instructions. In the support example, caching 40% of the input brings Claude Sonnet 5.5 from $800 to $648 a month, a saving of 19%. Anything that changes on every request, such as a timestamp near the top of the prompt, quietly breaks the cache.

Fallbacks, retries and promotions

The assistant on this site uses Gemini 3.8 Flash by default and falls back to an open-weight model on Groq when Gemini is unavailable. I wrote up that Gemini to Groq fallback separately. A fallback means part of your traffic runs on a different price list, and retries add calls. I also budget for Gemini 3.8 Flash at its January 2027 price, not the promotion, because an estimate built on a promo price stops being true on a known date.

Agents and batch jobs

Agent features multiply calls, so estimate requests per user action, not per click. A single "research this company" button can trigger a plan, several searches, a draft and a review. My OpenAI Agents API guide covers cost controls for that case. Work that can wait, like weekly reports, belongs in a batch job at half price.

Free tiers

The Gemini API free tier currently includes Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and Gemini 3.8 Flash at no charge, with rate limits, and Google's pricing page notes that free-tier content may be used to improve its products. That makes it a good place to prototype and measure your token counts. I would not put customer data through it, and I would not plan a launch around it, because limits and terms are set by the provider and can change.

Pricing your AI feature: margin and break-even

Cost per user only matters next to revenue per user. Continuing the support example on Claude Sonnet 5.5, suppose you charge $29 per user per month, have $2.50 per user of other variable costs (hosting, email, payment fees) and $500 of fixed monthly costs:

  • Revenue: 1,000 × $29 = $29,000
  • Total cost: $648 API + $2,500 variable + $500 fixed = $3,648
  • Gross margin: about 87%
  • Break-even price: $3.65 per user

The calculator shows the same figures and a plain verdict. A negative margin means the plan loses money at that price. A positive margin under 60% means usage or pricing may need tighter limits. Above that, the price covers estimated usage with room for overhead. These thresholds are my planning rule, not an industry standard.

Averages hide power users. If your top 10% of users send five times more requests, run the calculator again with their numbers, and decide whether you need a fair-use limit or a usage-based tier. I covered the billing side in Stripe per-seat billing for SaaS, and the SaaS Metrics Calculator handles MRR, LTV and CAC once the price is set.

One honest limitation: the calculator prices cached tokens at the read rate. It does not add Claude's one-time cache write premium or Gemini's hourly cache storage fee, so treat its output as a planning estimate and compare it with your first real invoice.

Practical takeaway

Before you choose a model on API pricing alone, work through this list:

  1. Measure real input and output tokens per request, including system prompt, history and thinking.
  2. Count API calls per user per month, not clicks.
  3. Try the cheapest model that meets your quality bar first.
  4. Cap output length and cache the stable part of every prompt.
  5. Budget at post-promotion prices, and check margin for heavy users separately.

You can run all of this in the free AI API Cost Calculator, which has presets for chat, support, summarising and document workflows. If you are planning an AI feature for a SaaS product and want a second opinion on the architecture and cost, get in touch.

item.title: Shopify AI Store Builder vs Custom App: Auto Social Images
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Mustafa
item.description: The Shopify AI store builder drafts your store. Here is the custom Shopify app I built to auto-generate branded social share images for every product.
item.content:encoded:
The Shopify AI store builder can turn a short description of your business into a working store draft in minutes. As co-founder of StartStorez, where our team has delivered more than 2,000 Shopify stores, I have watched that first step get much faster. The work that still eats a merchant's week usually starts after launch.

In this post I explain what the Shopify AI store builder does well and where it stops, then walk through a real custom Shopify app I built: a multi-store app that automatically creates branded social share images for every product, so links shared on WhatsApp and Facebook show the price and the deal instead of a plain photo. You will see the problem, the constraints, how it works and the trade-offs.

What the Shopify AI store builder does well, and where it stops

According to Shopify's own website builder page, you describe your business and the AI store builder generates store designs you can then edit with drag-and-drop tools. Sidekick, Shopify's built-in AI assistant, helps write product descriptions, headlines and customer messages. Shopify's AI website builder guide is clear that the result is a first draft: you still review layout, copy and SEO before publishing.

That is a real improvement for getting started. For a merchant moving from selling on Instagram to their own Shopify store, it removes the blank-page problem and the first few days of theme setup. But a store builder, AI or not, builds pages. It does not run your store's ongoing operations. Some jobs need logic that reacts to your own data every day.

OptionBest forLimit
Shopify AI store builderA fast first draft of layout, copy and designBuilds pages; does not automate store-specific workflows
Apps from the Shopify App StoreCommon needs such as reviews, bundles or emailYou adapt your process to the app's rules
Custom Shopify appA workflow specific to your products or business modelNeeds a Shopify developer and ongoing maintenance

My rule after years of store builds: start with the AI store builder and the App Store, and only build a custom app when a repeated manual task costs real hours every week and no existing app fits. The project below met that bar.

The problem: every shared product link looked the same

The store in this case sells daily deals, and most of its traffic comes from product links shared in WhatsApp groups and on Facebook. When someone shares a Shopify product link, the chat app shows a preview built from the page's Open Graph tags, usually just the product photo and title. The price, the discount and the brand were missing from the one image people actually saw.

Making a promotional image by hand for every product and every price change does not scale for a deals store. Two other problems made it worse:

  • Social apps cache previews. After a price change, WhatsApp and Facebook kept showing the old image.
  • Deal roundups. Some pages promote four products together and needed a combined preview, which no store builder or theme setting produces.

The constraints were just as important as the feature. The app had to work for more than one store, keep images in each merchant's own Shopify account, avoid editing theme code by hand, and handle store credentials securely.

How I built the custom Shopify app

The app is built with Node.js and Express, uses the Shopify GraphQL Admin API, App Bridge and a theme app extension, generates images with Sharp, stores installation records in PostgreSQL and runs on Vercel. Here is how the pieces fit.

Webhooks start the work

When a merchant creates or updates a product, Shopify sends a products/create or products/update webhook. Every webhook is verified before anything happens, because anyone can send a POST request to a public URL:

import crypto from "node:crypto";

// rawBody must be the exact bytes Shopify sent, not re-serialised JSON.
function isValidShopifyWebhook(rawBody, hmacHeader, appSecret) {
  const digest = crypto.createHmac("sha256", appSecret).update(rawBody).digest("base64");
  const received = Buffer.from(hmacHeader || "", "base64");
  const expected = Buffer.from(digest, "base64");
  return received.length === expected.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(received, expected);
}

Shopify can deliver the same webhook more than once, and most product saves do not change anything that appears in the image. So the app hashes the inputs that matter (title, prices, badge, product image, logo) and skips generation when the hash has not changed. That one check removed most of the unnecessary work.

Generating the image with Sharp

For a single product, the app builds a 1200 × 628 image with the product photo, a badge, the sale price, the crossed-out regular price and the store logo. For roundup pages, it builds a four-card layout from the products selected in a metafield. Merchants can override the badge text, prices and headline per product through metafields, or switch generation off for one product.

I chose Sharp over a headless browser screenshot because it is fast, predictable and cheap to run in a serverless function. The trade-off is that layout is done in code rather than HTML, so design changes take longer.

I also decided not to use a generative AI image model here, even though "AI" sells well. A deal image has to show the exact price, the exact logo and the same layout every time. Image models still get text and numbers wrong, and a wrong price in a shared link is worse than no image. AI is useful around this workflow, for example to suggest badge wording, but the image itself is built from the store's data.

Merchant-owned storage and metafields

Generated images are uploaded to the merchant's own Shopify Files, so they are served from Shopify's CDN and stay in the merchant's account if they ever uninstall the app. The image URL and version hashes are written back to product metafields in a single mutation. The app creates the metafield definitions during installation, so merchants never set them up by hand.

Beating the social preview cache

Facebook offers an API to force a re-scrape, but relying on it for every product change is fragile. Instead, the app stores a short sharing version, and a small theme app embed adds it to the shared product URL as a pv parameter. When the image changes, the version changes, the URL is new to the social app, and it fetches the fresh preview.

Installation and security

The app supports many stores. App Bridge provides signed session tokens, the backend exchanges them for offline access tokens, and those tokens are encrypted before they are stored per shop. It also implements Shopify's mandatory privacy webhooks and cleans up on uninstall. I wrote about the same webhook discipline for payments in Stripe webhooks: fixing duplicates and retries.

What the merchant actually does

All of this is hidden from the store owner. After installing the app, a merchant does four things:

  1. Installs the app and approves its Shopify permissions.
  2. Uploads a logo and confirms the public storefront domain.
  3. Opens the theme editor link, switches on the social preview embed and saves the theme.
  4. Saves a product. The promotional image is created automatically from then on.

That is the kind of hand-off I aim for with any Shopify build: the clever part runs in the background, and the store team keeps working in the Shopify admin they already know.

Trade-offs and what I would change

No custom build is free of compromises. These are the honest ones in this project:

  • One manual step remains. Shopify disables theme app embeds by default, so the merchant has to switch on the social preview embed and save the theme once.
  • Themes differ. Some themes already print their own Open Graph tags, so duplicate tags must be tested on each target theme before release.
  • Stricter duplicate tracking. The content hashes make repeated deliveries harmless, but storing each webhook delivery ID would be the stronger production design.
  • Distribution rules. Serving unrelated merchants needs public distribution and Shopify App Review; custom distribution is limited to one store or one organisation.
  • Testing limits. A password-protected development store cannot complete the final external crawler check, so that step happens on a live storefront.

AI store builder, app or custom build: how to decide

If you are starting a store, use the Shopify AI store builder for the first draft and spend your energy on products, photos and offers. Add apps from the App Store for common needs. Consider a custom Shopify app when all of these are true:

  1. The task repeats every day or every week and is done by hand today.
  2. It depends on your own data, such as product metafields, prices or inventory.
  3. No existing app does it the way your business works.
  4. Saving that time or improving that result is worth a build and ongoing maintenance.

The social image app met all four: every product change used to need a new image, the image depended on product data, and the result showed up in every shared link. You can see it with my other work in the portfolio. If you need a Shopify developer for a custom app or automation like this, get in touch and tell me what you are doing by hand today.

item.title: Claude Code vs Codex: Which AI Coding Agent Fits Real SaaS Work?
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Mustafa
item.description: Compare Claude Code vs Codex for real SaaS development, including repo context, permissions, long tasks, code review, pros, cons and best use cases.
item.content:encoded:
Claude Code vs Codex is one of the most useful AI coding agent comparisons in 2026, but most answers reduce it to a model leaderboard. That is not how I choose a tool for production SaaS work. The better question is whether the agent can understand the repository, respect its boundaries, make a narrow change, run the right checks and show enough evidence for a human to review the result.

I use coding agents around real work that includes a static portfolio with automated SEO validation, React and Next.js products, Node.js services, Angular applications and private client repositories. In those environments, a beautiful first answer matters less than a clean diff, correct tests and no accidental changes outside the requested scope.

This guide compares Claude Code and OpenAI Codex by workflow rather than hype. I cover repository instructions, permissions, long-running tasks, parallel work, code review, pros and cons, and a practical way to decide which one fits your project. Features and plans change quickly, so I link to official documentation and avoid declaring a permanent winner.

Claude Code vs Codex at a glance

Decision areaClaude CodeOpenAI Codex
Primary working styleTerminal-first interactive coding agentCLI, IDE, web, app and delegated cloud workflows
Repository guidanceCLAUDE.md and project settingsAGENTS.md, skills and project instructions
PermissionsTool allow and deny rules, permission modes and promptsSandbox boundaries, approval rules and configurable network access
Long tasksInteractive sessions, resumable conversations and print modeLocal collaboration plus isolated or background tasks
Best fitDevelopers who want a close terminal pairing loopDevelopers who want both pairing and delegated execution
Main riskGiving broad shell permissions to move fasterDelegating an unclear task and reviewing only the summary

Both can inspect code, edit files, run commands and use external tools. Neither can guarantee that generated code is correct, secure or maintainable. The quality of the repository instructions and verification loop still decides whether the result is useful.

The biggest difference is the working loop

Claude Code feels naturally centred on a terminal conversation. You start it inside a project, explain the task, inspect what it finds and continue the same session. Its CLI supports interactive work, one-shot print mode, JSON output for automation, session continuation and explicit model or permission choices. That makes it easy to keep a developer in the loop while the agent explores and edits.

Codex now covers more surfaces. The CLI and IDE extension support local collaboration, while cloud or app workflows can run isolated tasks and return changes for review. OpenAI describes Codex as useful for writing features, answering repository questions, fixing bugs and proposing pull requests. That wider surface is valuable when I want one task to continue while I inspect another, but it also makes task boundaries more important.

I would choose based on the loop I actually need. For an uncertain bug where I expect to steer every few minutes, a terminal-first session is comfortable. For a clear migration, test addition or repeated repository check, isolated delegation can reduce context switching.

CLAUDE.md vs AGENTS.md: context beats clever prompts

A coding agent joining an unfamiliar repository has the same problem as a new engineer: it does not know the local rules. Claude Code uses files such as CLAUDE.md and settings to carry project guidance. Codex uses AGENTS.md files and reusable skills. The filenames differ, but the principle is the same.

My useful repository instructions are operational. They say which files are generated, which command rebuilds CSS, which tests must pass, which untracked files belong to the user and whether a push is allowed. They also explain unusual choices that look like bugs, such as keeping relative paths for locally reviewed blog drafts.

# Repository rules
- Read the current branch and status before editing.
- Do not modify or delete unrelated untracked files.
- Rebuild CSS after changing Tailwind classes.
- Run focused tests plus the site SEO validator.
- Never push unless the user explicitly asks.

This context prevents more failures than a long one-off prompt. It also makes comparisons fairer. If Claude Code receives precise repository rules while Codex receives only “fix the page,” the result measures setup quality, not agent quality.

Permissions and sandboxing decide how safely the agent moves

Claude Code exposes tool permission controls, including allowed and disallowed tools, permission modes and a deliberately dangerous option that skips prompts. Its official CLI reference warns users to treat that bypass with caution. The practical advantage is fine control over the local interactive loop. The danger is that repeated prompts can tempt a developer to approve a broader rule than the task needs.

Codex emphasises sandboxed execution and approvals. OpenAI says Codex agents are limited by default to the working folder or branch and ask before higher-risk actions such as broader network access. In a real repository, that boundary is useful because reading a file, changing source code, publishing a site and sending an external message are not the same level of authority.

My rule for both tools is simple: begin read-only, inspect the exact target, allow writes only inside the intended workspace and separate deployment from implementation. I do not disable safeguards just to remove friction. The few seconds saved by a broad permission are not worth an accidental push, deleted asset or leaked secret.

Long tasks, parallel agents and code review

AI coding agents are most impressive when a task spans several files, but that is also where drift becomes expensive. A request such as “improve SEO” can quietly turn into title changes, content rewrites, new schema, image replacement and deployment. I prefer a measurable finish line: edit these files, preserve these interfaces, run these commands and stop if a required external choice appears.

Codex is particularly attractive when independent work can run in parallel or in an isolated environment. One task can research documentation while another inspects tests, provided they do not edit the same mutable files. Claude Code also supports subagents and strong long-horizon workflows, but I still avoid delegation when a small direct search or single-file edit is enough. Extra agents add cost and can duplicate conclusions.

For either product, the final review should start with the diff, not the agent summary. I check whether the requested files changed, whether generated files were rebuilt, whether unrelated formatting moved and whether tests prove the actual behaviour. I also verify the user-facing production page after deployment. A green local test does not prove that the correct build reached the correct domain.

Claude Code pros and cons

Where Claude Code fits well

  • Terminal pairing: the interactive loop is direct for exploration, debugging and incremental implementation.
  • Scriptable output: print mode and JSON output make focused automation possible.
  • Explicit tool controls: allowed and disallowed tool rules can match a team’s workflow.
  • Session continuity: continuing or resuming work helps when a problem needs several passes.
  • MCP support: external tools and data can be connected through a standard protocol.

Claude Code trade-offs

  • A fast local loop can encourage over-broad shell permissions.
  • Long sessions still need written state and narrow acceptance criteria.
  • Model choice, usage limits and cost can change, so old comparisons age quickly.
  • A convincing explanation can still hide an unnecessarily large diff.

Codex pros and cons

Where Codex fits well

  • Multiple surfaces: local CLI and IDE work can sit beside cloud or app delegation.
  • Sandbox-first workflow: isolated execution supports clearer workspace boundaries.
  • Evidence-driven delivery: terminal logs, tests and file citations make results easier to inspect.
  • Repository instructions: AGENTS.md can preserve project rules close to the code.
  • Reusable skills: repeatable workflows can be packaged instead of pasted into every prompt.

Codex trade-offs

  • Delegation works poorly when the task itself is vague.
  • Parallel work needs clean ownership to avoid conflicting edits.
  • Approval and sandbox settings require deliberate configuration.
  • The wider product surface can feel heavier than a simple terminal session.

Can Claude Code and Codex work together?

Yes, but I would not ask both to rewrite the same feature and then choose whichever output looks nicer. A better pattern separates responsibilities. One agent can inspect architecture or review a plan. The other can implement a bounded change. A cross-review can then look for missed tests, unsafe assumptions or unnecessary complexity.

That review is useful only when the agents receive the same requirements and the human checks the disagreement. Two confident answers are not independent proof. For algorithm discussions, I also use my free JavaScript Big O Complexity Coach to show detected loops, sorts and allocations instead of accepting an unsupported O(1) claim.

For tool integration decisions beyond coding agents, see my MCP vs REST API comparison for AI agents. The same principle applies: choose the smallest interface that solves the real workflow.

Which AI coding agent should you choose?

Choose Claude Code first when you want a close terminal partner, expect frequent steering and value a simple interactive flow. Choose Codex first when you want local work plus isolated delegation, reusable skills and a stronger separation between implementation and review environments.

For a team, run a small evaluation on your own repository. Use one bug fix, one refactor and one test-writing task. Give both agents the same instructions, permissions and time. Measure accepted diff size, human review time, test quality, regressions and total cost. Do not score only whether the first attempt “worked.”

I would also avoid locking a permanent company decision to one model release. Store project rules in the repository, keep tests portable and make the review process independent from the agent. That makes it easier to switch tools when pricing, models or security requirements change.

Practical takeaway

There is no universal winner in Claude Code vs Codex. Claude Code is a strong fit for terminal-first collaboration. Codex is a strong fit for a mix of local pairing and delegated, sandboxed work. Both become much more reliable when the repository contains clear instructions and the task has a narrow definition of done.

Read the official Claude Code setup guide, Claude Code CLI reference, OpenAI Codex overview and Codex app announcement before deciding from a feature table that may go stale.

If you need a senior full-stack developer to build or review a production SaaS or AI workflow, tell me what you are building.

item.title: How to Submit Your Site to Bing with IndexNow (2026 Guide)
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Mustafa
item.description: Submit your site to Bing the right way: verify it in Bing Webmaster Tools, add an IndexNow key, read response codes and automate pings on each deploy.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to submit your site to Bing, there are two separate jobs. First, prove to Bing that you own the site and give it a sitemap, so it knows every page you want indexed. Second, tell Bing quickly whenever a page is added or changed. Bing Webmaster Tools handles the first job. IndexNow handles the second.

In this guide I walk through both, using the setup I run on this portfolio site: a static site on Netlify that sends an IndexNow ping automatically after every production deploy. I also cover the response codes you will see, the mistakes that waste effort, and one thing IndexNow does not do at all: it does not notify Google.

What IndexNow is and why it matters for Bing

Search engines normally find changes by crawling: a bot visits your pages on its own schedule and checks what is new. On a small or young site, that schedule can be slow.

IndexNow reverses the direction. Your site sends a short message that says "these exact URLs changed." According to the IndexNow FAQ, the participating engines include Bing, Yandex, Naver, Seznam.cz, Yep and Amazon, and the IndexNow documentation says a submission is shared with all of them. You only submit once.

Google is not on that list. For Google, you still rely on your sitemap and Google Search Console. This is the most common misunderstanding I see.

There is also a newer reason to care. In February 2026, Microsoft introduced AI Performance in Bing Webmaster Tools, a report showing how often your pages are cited in Microsoft Copilot and AI-generated summaries in Bing. The same announcement recommends IndexNow so AI systems can reference the current version of your content.

One honest limit: submitting a URL does not guarantee indexing. Each engine still decides whether to crawl and index the page.

Step 1: Add and verify your site in Bing Webmaster Tools

Verification proves you control the site, and the sitemap gives Bing a complete list of pages to start from.

  1. Sign in to Bing Webmaster Tools.
  2. Import from Google Search Console if you can. If your site is already verified there, the Import option lets Bing read your verified sites and their sitemaps, so you skip a second verification. Bing's import guide notes that Bing re-checks ownership through that connection from time to time. If you later revoke access, you will need another verification method.
  3. Otherwise, add the URL manually and verify it with an XML file, a meta tag or a DNS record, as described in Bing's add and verify guide.
  4. Submit your sitemap in the Sitemaps section, for example https://example.com/sitemap.xml.
  5. Check that Bing read it. The sitemap status should show success and a discovered URL count close to the number of pages you expect.

Keep the sitemap clean. Mine lists only pages I want in search results, so drafts and the contact form's thank-you page are left out. This matters later, because my IndexNow automation uses the sitemap as its allow-list.

Expect quiet reports at first. On a young domain some Bing reports stay empty for a while. When I wrote this, my own site still showed no backlink data in Bing, which is normal for a new domain and not a setup error.

Step 2: Create an IndexNow key and host the key file

The key is how IndexNow checks that the person sending URLs controls the website. You choose it yourself.

  1. Create a key between 8 and 128 characters, using letters, numbers and dashes. A random 32-character hexadecimal string works well.
  2. Create a text file named after the key, such as a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8.txt. It should contain only the key and be saved as UTF-8.
  3. Upload it to your site root, so it loads at https://example.com/a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8.txt.
  4. Open that URL in a browser and confirm you see the key and nothing else.

The root location matters. A key file at the root covers every URL on that host. In a subfolder, you must send its address as keyLocation, and it only covers URLs inside that folder. Each subdomain also needs its own key file.

The key is not a password. Anyone can read the file by design; it only proves that whoever submits URLs can also place files on your site.

Two details came up while I built the key check for my IndexNow Submitter tool. Some Windows editors add an invisible byte order mark (BOM) to the start of UTF-8 files, so a file that looks correct can fail an exact comparison. My checker removes it before comparing. I also made the checker reject redirects. If your host redirects the key file, fix the file location instead of hoping every engine follows the redirect.

Step 3: Submit changed URLs and read the response

For a single URL, a GET request is enough. The url value should be URL-encoded:

https://api.indexnow.org/indexnow?url=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fblog%2Fnew-post.html&key=a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8

For several URLs, send one POST request with JSON. The documentation allows up to 10,000 URLs in a single request.

const response = await fetch("https://api.indexnow.org/indexnow", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8" },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    host: "example.com",
    key: "a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8",
    keyLocation: "https://example.com/a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8.txt",
    urlList: [
      "https://example.com/blog/new-post.html",
      "https://example.com/pricing.html",
    ],
  }),
});

console.log(response.status);

The HTTP status code tells you what happened:

CodeMeaningWhat to do
200The URLs were received.Nothing. Wait for the crawl.
202The URLs were received, but the key is still being validated.Normal on a first submission. Confirm the key file loads.
400The request format is invalid.Check the JSON fields and URL encoding.
403The key is not valid. The file was not found, or it does not contain the key.Open the key file URL and compare it with the key you sent.
422The URLs do not belong to the host, or the key does not follow the protocol rules.Make sure every URL uses the same host as host, including www.
429Too many requests.Slow down and stop resending the same URLs.

If you would rather not write code, I built a free IndexNow Submitter that generates a key, checks your key file and sends your URLs from the browser. It uses a small server function because the IndexNow API does not accept direct calls from web pages on other sites. It sits alongside my other free developer tools.

How I automated IndexNow on a Netlify static site

Manual submission works until someone forgets it. I update this site several times a week, so I wanted the ping to happen inside the deploy, without ever sending unchanged pages.

The IndexNow FAQ asks you to submit only meaningful changes, so sending the whole sitemap on every deploy was not an option. Instead, I wrote a small local Netlify build plugin that runs on the onSuccess event, after the deploy is live. Netlify's build plugin documentation notes that this event cannot stop a deploy, which is what I want: a failed ping should never block a release.

The plugin follows four rules:

  1. Run only in the production context, so branch previews and draft deploys never send a ping.
  2. Compare the previous production commit with the new one, using the CACHED_COMMIT_REF and COMMIT_REF values from Netlify's build environment variables.
  3. Turn changed HTML files into URLs and keep only the ones listed in sitemap.xml.
  4. Catch every error, show it in the deploy summary and let the deploy finish.

The core is short. This is a simplified version of the real code:

# netlify.toml
[[plugins]]
  package = "/netlify/plugins/indexnow"

// netlify/plugins/indexnow/changed-urls.js (simplified)
if (process.env.CONTEXT !== "production") return skip("not production");
const { CACHED_COMMIT_REF: from, COMMIT_REF: to } = process.env;
if (!from || from === to) return skip("no new commit");
const changedFiles = git(["diff", "--name-only", "--diff-filter=AMR", from, to]);
const urls = toUrls(changedFiles).filter((url) => sitemapUrls.has(url));

The whole handler sits in a try/catch, and errors go to the deploy summary through utils.status.show. After the first deploy with the plugin, that summary showed "IndexNow: Submitted 2 changed URL(s), HTTP 200." Each production deploy now reports the URLs it sent or the reason it skipped.

Trade-offs I accepted

The plugin only looks at HTML files. A shared stylesheet change sends nothing, because the content did not change. That matches the purpose of IndexNow.

It also ignores deleted files. The protocol lets you submit removed URLs, but I rarely delete pages. When I retire one, I add a 301 redirect and send the old address manually.

One Netlify detail is easy to miss. When a build runs without cache, CACHED_COMMIT_REF equals COMMIT_REF, so the plugin skips. For those cases I keep npm run indexnow:submit as a manual fallback.

Mistakes that waste your IndexNow effort

Most IndexNow problems are not technical. They come from expecting the protocol to do something it was not built for.

  • Expecting Google to react. Google is not a participant. Use Search Console and an accurate sitemap for Google.
  • Resubmitting everything on every deploy. Send only pages whose content changed. A 429 response is a clear sign that you are sending too much.
  • Using IndexNow as a backfill. It is for changes from now on. Your sitemap covers older pages.
  • Sending pages that should not be indexed. Drafts, preview links and noindex pages do not belong in a submission. A sitemap filter prevents this.
  • Mixing hosts. If the key file is on example.com but the URLs use www.example.com, expect a 422. Pick one main host and redirect the other to it.
  • Treating 202 as an error. It usually means the key is still being checked. Confirm the key file loads and wait, instead of generating a new key.

After setup, check Bing Webmaster Tools. URL Inspection shows whether a page is indexed, and AI Performance shows whether your pages are cited in Copilot answers. The reports a few days later tell you more than a single submission response.

Practical takeaway

To submit your site to Bing properly, treat it as two layers. Verify the site in Bing Webmaster Tools and submit a clean sitemap once. Then use IndexNow for every meaningful change after that, ideally from your deploy pipeline so nobody has to remember it. Keep Google on its own track through Search Console.

If you only want to test the protocol, start with the IndexNow Submitter and one URL. If you want the same automation added to your website or SaaS deploy pipeline, get in touch and tell me how your site is built and deployed.

item.title: MCP vs REST API for AI Agents: When to Use Each
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Mustafa
item.description: Compare MCP vs REST API for AI agents, including architecture, pros and cons, security, tool discovery, and when a hybrid approach works best.
item.content:encoded:
MCP vs REST API is often presented as a choice between an old integration style and a new one for AI agents. That framing is misleading. A REST API gives application code a predictable way to access data and operations. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, gives an AI client a standard way to discover and call tools, read resources and understand what a server offers.

In many production systems, the right answer is not MCP or REST. It is a stable service layer exposed through REST for normal applications, with an MCP adapter added when an AI host needs tool discovery and model-friendly descriptions.

I use this distinction in my own SaaS work. The Ask Mustafa assistant on this site calls a normal serverless HTTP endpoint. The server owns provider selection, secrets, validation and error handling. If I later wanted external AI hosts to discover portfolio or service tools, I would expose carefully scoped MCP operations over the same trusted application logic. I would not rebuild the product around a protocol just because it is popular.

This guide compares MCP and REST APIs, explains their pros and cons, covers the 2026 MCP changes, and gives a practical decision framework for AI agents and SaaS products.

MCP vs REST API at a glance

The shortest answer is that REST describes how software clients work with resources over HTTP, while MCP standardises how AI applications discover and use context and capabilities. They can use similar infrastructure, but they solve different integration problems.

Decision areaREST APIMCP server
Primary callerApplication code written by developersAI hosts and agent clients
Operation discoveryDocumentation or OpenAPI at design timeProtocol methods and tool metadata at runtime
Typical contractURLs, HTTP methods, status codes and schemasTools, resources, prompts and JSON schemas
Control flowCode decides which endpoint to callA model may select a tool within client controls
Best fitWeb apps, mobile apps, services and partner integrationsAI assistants that need portable access to tools and context
Main riskBreaking clients or weak endpoint authorizationOver-broad tools, unsafe model decisions and trust-boundary mistakes

Neither side automatically makes a system secure, fast or easy to maintain. Those outcomes still depend on clear contracts, narrow permissions, input validation, idempotency, observability and careful product design.

What a REST API does well

A REST API is useful when the calling code already knows the operation it needs. A checkout page calls a payment endpoint. A dashboard requests an organisation's reports. A mobile application updates a delivery status. The developer chooses the URL, HTTP method, headers, request body and response handling before the software runs.

The official HTTP semantics specification defines a stateless request and response model with shared meanings for methods and status codes. That predictability matters. Gateways, caches, monitoring tools, client libraries and engineering teams already understand it.

REST API advantages

  • Direct control: application code decides exactly when an operation runs.
  • Mature infrastructure: authentication, rate limiting, caching, tracing and testing tools are widely available.
  • Clear client contracts: OpenAPI documents endpoints and schemas for developers and generated clients.
  • Broad compatibility: almost any platform can send an HTTPS request.
  • Efficient product interfaces: a purpose-built endpoint can return only the data a known screen needs.

REST API limitations for AI agents

A raw API description is not always enough for a model. An endpoint named POST /cases/{id}/actions may be clear to the team that built it but ambiguous to an agent. The model needs to understand what the action changes, which arguments are safe, whether approval is required and how to interpret failures.

Teams often solve that problem with custom function definitions, prompt instructions and adapter code for every AI client. That can work, especially for one internal assistant, but the integration becomes harder to reuse across different hosts.

What MCP adds for AI agents

MCP gives AI applications a shared protocol for discovering and invoking capabilities. A server can expose tools for actions, resources for readable context and prompts for reusable interaction patterns. An MCP-compatible host can inspect these definitions instead of relying on a separate one-off connector for every service.

The official July 2026 MCP specification introduced a stateless protocol core. Modern requests carry their protocol version and client information with each call, and remote servers no longer require the older initialisation handshake or protocol-level session. The release also added header-based routing, cacheable list results and authorization hardening. That makes current MCP easier to operate on ordinary HTTP infrastructure than descriptions based on older session behaviour suggest.

MCP advantages

  • Runtime discovery: an AI client can learn which tools and resources are currently available.
  • Model-facing descriptions: names, schemas and descriptions can explain when a capability should be used.
  • Portable integrations: one server can work with multiple compatible AI hosts.
  • Risk vocabulary: tool annotations can describe read-only, destructive, idempotent and open-world behaviour.
  • Context and actions together: the same protocol can provide readable resources and callable tools.

MCP limitations

MCP does not remove the underlying API, database or business service. A tool still needs real code to search records, create a draft or update a ticket. It also adds another public contract to version, secure, test and monitor.

Tool descriptions are not authorization. A model may misunderstand a description, select the wrong tool or repeat a call after a timeout. The official MCP maintainers describe annotations as hints, not guarantees. Deterministic controls must still verify identity, tenant, scope, arguments and approval at execution time.

MCP is also unnecessary when a small application has one fixed server call and no need for portable discovery. Adding a protocol layer to a simple form submission can create more maintenance without improving the user experience.

Use REST and MCP together instead of rebuilding everything

The architecture I prefer keeps business logic independent from both transports. A service function enforces permissions, validates input and performs the operation. A REST route calls that function for the web or mobile application. An MCP tool calls the same function for an approved AI host.

async function createSupportDraft(input, actor) {
  await requirePermission(actor, input.caseId, 'case:draft')
  const safeInput = DraftSchema.parse(input)
  return supportService.createDraft(safeInput, actor.id)
}

rest.post('/cases/:id/draft', async (request) => {
  return createSupportDraft(request.body, request.user)
})

mcp.registerTool('create_support_draft', toolSchema, async (args, context) => {
  return createSupportDraft(args, context.user)
})

This is deliberately framework-neutral pseudocode. The important point is the boundary: neither the REST route nor the MCP registration owns the authorization rule. Both enter the same tested service layer.

Do not expose every endpoint as a tool

Automatically converting a large OpenAPI file into hundreds of MCP tools may look efficient, but it can give the model too many overlapping choices. Design agent tools around clear tasks. A tool named prepare_refund_review can be safer than separate low-level tools for loading a payment, loading a customer, calculating fees and changing a status.

Keep high-impact execution narrow. Read tools can retrieve a small approved view. Draft tools can prepare changes without applying them. Write tools can require explicit confirmation and server-side idempotency. Destructive actions should be rare, obvious and separately authorized.

Security and operations differ at the decision layer

REST and MCP can share TLS, OAuth, gateways, logs and rate limits. The extra MCP risk comes from placing a probabilistic model between user intent and tool selection. The server must assume that a syntactically valid call can still be inappropriate.

For every tool, define the allowed caller, tenant scope, data fields, side effects, retry behaviour and approval rule. Validate access tokens for the intended server. Never accept a token merely because another upstream service accepted it. Treat tool output and external resources as untrusted input before returning them to a model.

Make writes idempotent where possible. If a client times out after creating an invoice or ticket, a retry should not create a duplicate. Use a stable operation key, record the result and return the existing outcome when the same authorised request arrives again.

Logs should connect the user request, selected tool, validated actor, tenant, operation key, result and latency without storing secrets or unnecessary private content. My MCP server security checklist covers tool permissions, prompt injection, token handling and audit evidence in more detail. The security principles apply globally even though that article also discusses UAE deployment considerations.

MCP vs REST API decision checklist

Choose a REST API as the primary interface when:

  • a web, mobile or service client has a known workflow;
  • developers need direct control over every request;
  • partners expect HTTP endpoints and OpenAPI documentation;
  • caching and resource semantics are central to the design;
  • an AI feature uses only one or two fixed internal calls.

Add an MCP server when:

  • several AI hosts need access to the same approved capabilities;
  • runtime tool or resource discovery provides real value;
  • the model must choose between a small set of clearly described operations;
  • you can expose narrow tasks without bypassing application authorization;
  • the team can maintain protocol versions, evaluations and tool-level monitoring.

Use both when the product already has a reliable API and now needs agent access. Keep REST for deterministic applications and partner integrations. Put a curated MCP layer in front of selected service operations. This preserves the mature API while giving AI clients a standard contract.

Practical takeaway

MCP does not replace REST APIs. REST remains a strong foundation for predictable software integration. MCP adds a model-friendly layer for discovering tools, reading context and calling approved capabilities from compatible AI hosts.

Start with the caller and the decision. If your own code knows exactly what to call, use the API directly. If an AI host needs portable discovery across several carefully scoped capabilities, MCP may earn its extra operational cost. For many SaaS products, the best design is a shared service layer with both REST and MCP adapters.

Read the official 2026-07-28 MCP specification release, the maintainers' tool annotations guidance, and RFC 9110 HTTP semantics before fixing the production contract.

If you need help designing a secure AI agent, REST API or MCP integration for a SaaS product, contact me.

item.title: Firestore vs Supabase for Offline-First React Apps
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Mustafa
item.description: Compare Firestore and Supabase for offline-first React apps, including sync, security, data modelling, costs, lock-in and production trade-offs.
item.content:encoded:
Firestore vs Supabase for offline-first React apps is not simply a choice between NoSQL and PostgreSQL. The bigger question is how the product should behave when a device loses its connection, a user keeps working, and several queued changes reach the server later. Firestore gives client applications built-in offline persistence and synchronization. Supabase gives developers a relational PostgreSQL foundation, but a serious offline workflow normally needs another local database or synchronization layer.

I have worked with both sides in different products. Apex Logistics uses React, TanStack Query, Firestore and PWA support, while BWL League uses Supabase, PostgreSQL and Row Level Security. This is not a controlled benchmark between identical applications. It is a practical comparison of the architecture decisions that became important in real product work.

I will compare data modelling, offline writes, reconnect behaviour, security, cost risk and vendor lock-in. The right answer depends less on which platform has the longer feature list and more on the failure modes your users cannot accept.

Firestore vs Supabase for offline-first React apps: the core difference

Firestore is a managed document database inside Firebase. Data lives in collections and documents, with subcollections for deeper structures. Its web and mobile SDKs are designed around real-time listeners, cached data and direct client access protected by Security Rules. This makes it quick to build a React screen that continues showing previously loaded records when the network disappears.

Supabase is built around PostgreSQL. Data lives in tables with relationships, constraints, indexes, SQL functions and transactions. Supabase adds authentication, storage, real-time subscriptions and an API generated from the database schema. Client applications can query that API directly when Row Level Security is configured correctly.

The official Firestore data-model guide describes the collection and document structure. The Supabase architecture guide explains how its services sit around PostgreSQL. Those foundations affect almost every later decision.

DecisionFirestoreSupabase
Primary modelCollections and JSON-like documentsRelational PostgreSQL tables
Client offline supportBuilt into supported client SDKsUsually added through a local database or sync layer
AuthorizationFirebase Security RulesPostgreSQL Row Level Security
Complex relationshipsOften denormalized or handled in application codeNatural fit for joins, constraints and transactions
PortabilityTied closely to Firebase APIs and data modelPostgreSQL data and SQL are more portable

Firestore favours fast client development

Firestore feels natural when the application revolves around records that can be loaded independently: delivery stops, messages, field reports or user preferences. Real-time listeners and local caching reduce the amount of synchronization code needed for common cases. The trade-off is that relational reporting, cross-document consistency and complex filtering require careful modelling.

Supabase favours relational integrity

Supabase is usually easier when the domain has strong relationships: organizations, teams, memberships, roles, invoices and audit records. Foreign keys and database constraints can reject invalid states even when an application bug reaches the API. The trade-off is that PostgreSQL alone does not make the browser offline-first.

Offline reads and writes are the deciding factor

The official Firestore offline documentation says the client can read, write, listen to and query cached data. When connectivity returns, local changes synchronize with the backend. On the web, persistent caching must be enabled, supported browsers matter, and cached data may remain between sessions. That last point deserves a product decision on shared or sensitive devices.

Firestore also documents last-write-wins behaviour when several offline changes affect the same document. That rule is convenient, but it is not enough for every business operation. Two drivers updating a delivery note may tolerate a newer value replacing an older one. Two users consuming the last available inventory item need a stronger server-side check.

I still separate a friendly offline interface from a trustworthy business command. The UI can optimistically show a queued action, but the backend remains responsible for validating permissions, stock, status transitions and idempotency. A green check mark should mean accepted by the server, not merely saved on the device.

Supabase does not offer the same transparent browser persistence through its standard JavaScript client. Its official integration directory presents PowerSync as a PostgreSQL-to-SQLite synchronization layer for offline-first applications. Other teams use a local database, IndexedDB or their own operation queue. These approaches can work well, but conflict rules, schema changes and failed writes become explicit parts of the architecture.

For a web application, TanStack Query can cache server state and improve retry behaviour, but its cache should not be confused with a complete durable sync engine. In my offline-first React PWA guide, I cover persisted query data, mutation queues, idempotency and reconnect testing in more detail.

A small queue entry should describe business intent instead of storing an arbitrary HTTP request:

type PendingOperation = {
  id: string;
  entityId: string;
  action: "confirm-delivery" | "add-note";
  payload: Record<string, unknown>;
  createdAt: string;
  expectedVersion?: number;
};

The stable operation ID lets the server process a retry safely. The expected version can reveal that the record changed while the device was offline. Whether the backend is Firestore or Supabase, this is more reliable than blindly replaying requests.

Compare security, queries, cost and lock-in

Firebase Security Rules vs Supabase RLS

Firestore Security Rules evaluate access to document paths for mobile and web clients. Rules can use authentication claims and document data, but queries must be compatible with the rules because Firestore does not use them as filters. The official Security Rules guide also warns against open development rules in production.

Supabase Row Level Security applies policies inside PostgreSQL. A policy can limit which rows a user may select, insert, update or delete. That is a strong fit for organization and team boundaries, but a missing or overly broad policy can expose data. I treat RLS policies as production code, keep them in migrations and test both allowed and denied operations. The current Supabase RLS documentation recommends testing each operation for anonymous and authenticated roles.

My Supabase RLS guide for multi-role apps explains the team-isolation problems that appear when one user can hold different roles. Firestore can model the same business rules, but the implementation follows document paths and claims instead of SQL policies.

Queries and reporting

Firestore rewards query-driven denormalization. If a dashboard needs the same organization name on many records, copying that value may be simpler than rebuilding it through multiple reads. This improves a common screen but creates an update problem when shared data changes.

Supabase lets PostgreSQL perform joins, aggregations and transactional updates. That is valuable for admin reporting and domains with many relationships. It can also encourage an overly large query, so indexes, pagination and measured query plans still matter.

Cost and vendor lock-in

I would not choose either platform from a sample monthly bill. Firestore charges are strongly influenced by document reads, writes, deletes, storage and network use. A real-time listener or inefficient list screen can change the pattern. Supabase plans combine allocated compute and quotas with usage-based charges for some resources. Database size, bandwidth, real-time connections, storage and extra compute all matter.

Before launch, I estimate costs from product actions: opening a dashboard, syncing one shift, uploading evidence, generating a report and reconnecting after several hours. Then I test those actions with realistic data. The official Firestore pricing guide and Supabase pricing page should be checked again when the product is ready to launch because limits and prices can change.

Firestore creates more platform-specific code around listeners, rules, indexes and document modelling. Supabase is also a platform, but PostgreSQL data, SQL migrations and common database tools give a clearer exit path. Self-hosting Supabase is possible, though operating it safely is real infrastructure work, not a free portability button.

Firestore vs Supabase pros and cons: which should you choose?

Choose Firestore when

  • Reliable mobile or browser offline behaviour is a core requirement.
  • The data fits independent documents and predictable query patterns.
  • Real-time client updates matter more than complex relational reporting.
  • The team wants a managed backend and accepts Firebase-specific APIs.

Firestore pros: mature client SDKs, built-in offline persistence, real-time listeners and low backend setup for common app flows.

Firestore cons: denormalization work, platform-specific security and query rules, last-write-wins conflicts, and cost patterns that can surprise read-heavy screens.

Choose Supabase when

  • The product depends on organizations, memberships, roles and relational integrity.
  • SQL reporting, joins, constraints and transactions are central requirements.
  • PostgreSQL portability matters more than built-in client synchronization.
  • The team can add and operate a deliberate offline layer where needed.

Supabase pros: PostgreSQL, strong relational modelling, database-level RLS, SQL tooling and a more portable data foundation.

Supabase cons: offline synchronization needs additional architecture, RLS has a learning curve, and self-hosting adds operational responsibility.

For a field logistics PWA that must keep working during long connection gaps, I would usually start the evaluation with Firestore. For a multi-tenant SaaS dashboard with complex roles, reporting and relational workflows, I would usually start with Supabase. If the product needs both, I would first challenge whether every screen truly needs offline writes. Adding two primary data platforms normally creates more synchronization risk than it removes.

The best proof is a small failure-focused prototype. Put a device offline, make conflicting changes, close the browser, sign in as another user, reconnect slowly and inspect what the server finally accepts. That exercise exposes more than a polished feature matrix.

If you are planning an offline React product or choosing its backend, contact me. I can help turn the product requirements into a practical architecture before the expensive assumptions reach production.

item.title: Gemini API Fallback for 429 Errors with Groq in Node.js
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Mustafa
item.description: Build a Gemini API fallback for 429 and timeout errors using Groq, Node.js provider routing, Netlify secrets, safe logging and automated failover tests.
item.content:encoded:
A Gemini API fallback becomes important the first time a working chatbot hits a rate limit, times out, or receives a temporary provider error. A single model call can look reliable in local testing and still fail when real visitors arrive, a quota changes, or an upstream service becomes overloaded.

I recently added this pattern to the Ask Mustafa assistant on my portfolio. Gemini is the primary provider, Groq is the automatic fallback, and the server returns which provider answered so I can verify the production path. If the Gemini key is removed later, the same routing code continues with Groq without a frontend change.

This guide explains the practical decisions behind that implementation: which failures should be retried, when a request should move to the second provider, how to keep prompts and conversation history consistent, how to protect keys in Netlify Functions, and how to test failover without waiting for a real outage.

Why a Gemini API fallback is different from a retry

A retry sends the request to Gemini again. A fallback sends it to another provider. Those actions solves different problems, and treating them as the same thing can make an outage worse.

Google documents 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED for rate limits and recommends exponential backoff for retryable errors such as 429, 408, and 5xx responses. A short retry can help when capacity is temporarily unavailable. It does not help when a project has exhausted its daily allowance, billing is blocked, the selected model is unavailable to that project, or the request keeps exceeding the provider timeout.

A user-facing chatbot also has a latency budget. Four long retries may eventually succeed, but a visitor will experience the assistant as broken. I prefer a small, explicit timeout and a limited retry policy, followed by a second provider when the error is genuinely recoverable.

Classify the status before switching providers

  • 429: retry briefly when the response indicates a temporary limit, then fall back if the user cannot wait.
  • 408, 500, 502, 503, or 504: treat as temporary network or upstream failures. A bounded retry or fallback is reasonable.
  • 400: fix the payload, model parameters, or conversation format. Sending the same invalid request to another provider may hide a bug.
  • 401 or 403: investigate credentials, project access, billing, or policy restrictions. Do not rotate through providers indefinitely.
  • Safety refusal: preserve the refusal. A fallback must never be used to bypass a provider safety decision.

The exact policy depend on the product. A background summary can wait and retry. A support widget needs a quick answer or an honest temporary error. The routing layer should know that difference.

Build one provider contract in Node.js

The frontend should not contain Gemini-specific or Groq-specific logic inside it. It should send one request to a server endpoint and receive one normalized answer. The server owns provider order, authentication, timeouts, error mapping, and observability.

I use a small provider contract with the same inputs for both services: a system prompt, the current question, recent conversation history, environment variables, and a fetch implementation. Each adapter translates those shared inputs into the provider's request format and returns plain answer text.

async function generateAnswer({ systemPrompt, question, history, env, fetchImpl }) {
  const order = env.AI_PRIMARY_PROVIDER === "groq"
    ? ["groq", "gemini"]
    : ["gemini", "groq"];

  const enabled = order.filter((provider) =>
    provider === "gemini" ? env.GEMINI_API_KEY : env.GROQ_API_KEY
  );

  let lastError;
  for (const provider of enabled) {
    try {
      const answer = provider === "gemini"
        ? await callGemini({ systemPrompt, question, history, env, fetchImpl })
        : await callGroq({ systemPrompt, question, history, env, fetchImpl });
      return { answer, provider };
    } catch (error) {
      lastError = normalizeProviderError(provider, error);
      logSafeFailure(lastError.provider, lastError.code);
    }
  }

  throw lastError;
}

This loop is intentionally boring. Reliability code should be easy to read during an incident. Adding a third provider later should mean adding one adapter and one configuration entry, not rewriting the chatbot.

Keep provider differences inside the adapters

Gemini and Groq do not use identical request bodies. Gemini represents conversation content as user and model roles with parts. Groq exposes an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions shape. Their token controls, model names, error bodies, and response structures also differ.

The adapter should absorb those differences. The rest of the application should not depend on candidates[0].content.parts or choices[0].message.content. It should receive a validated non-empty string or a normalized error.

That boundary also protects future migrations. A provider can change a model name or SDK without forcing a change to the browser, prompt builder, or knowledge-selection code.

Preserve behaviour when the provider changes

Successful failover is not only an HTTP 200 response. The fallback answer must still follow the product rules.

For Ask Mustafa, both providers receive the same verified portfolio context, system instructions, user question, and recent history. The prompt blocks fabricated prices, availability, client results, and unsupported experience. Scope Doctor mode has a different structured prompt, but it follows the same provider route.

I keep temperature and output limits conservative, validate the returned text, and apply a final server-side length cap. The fallback should not suddenly produce a long essay when the primary normally returns a short answer.
